title: KV-cache memory sharding protocol across tensor & pipeline parallel ranks
creator: Aisha Malik
description:
Summary:
Design and implement a memory-efficient, low-latency protocol for sharding KV cache across multi-GPU inference setups that mix tensor parallel (TP) and pipeline parallel (PP). Goal is to reduce peak GPU memory usage for KV cache on long-context workloads while preserving/ improving latency for streaming continuous-batching use-cases.

Background and motivation:
- Long-context streaming customers are the largest driver of KV cache memory growth. Current single-GPU KV replication limits maximum context length and forces expensive model quantization or smaller batch sizes.
- Past experiment ENG-7420 explored KV sharding strategies but left open the runtime protocol when TP and PP are both in use (tensor shards inside a pipeline stage). We need a general protocol that composes with our kernel selection, continuous batching, and our smart routing fallback model variants.

Design goals (ranked):
1) Bounded per-GPU memory for KV cache (deterministic upper bound given config).
2) Minimal extra cross-GPU bandwidth in the common case (streaming single-request, many small tokens).
3) Latency-friendly for tail P95/P99 of token generation under continuous batching.
4) Compatibility with existing TP/PP placement (no mandatory topology re-mapping).
5) Graceful fallbacks to CPU-hosted KV and transparent eviction/rehydration.

Key constraints and trade-offs considered:
- If we shard KV by head ranges (attention-head sharding), we reduce memory per GPU but require reduce-scatter + all-gather of attention outputs per token step which increases interconnect bandwidth and latency for small token sizes.
- If we shard KV by token-sequence slices (time sharding), streaming generation requires fetching remote time slices for new tokens and may induce many small point-to-point transfers when prefix tokens are cached on different GPUs.
- Hybrid: a two-level mapping (token-blocks x head-blocks) to balance bandwidth across NCCL links; increases complexity in index mapping and eviction.

Selected approach (protocol overview):
1) Topology-aware block-sharding: split KV into contiguous token-blocks (configurable block_size_tokens, default 256) and attention-head blocks (head_block_size, default equal split across TP ranks). Each GPU is assigned a set of (token_block_idx, head_block_idx) tuples based on physical placement and intra-node NVLink topology.
2) Local fast-path: For generation steps that only need KV local blocks (common when prefix fits in local blocks), runtime proceeds with no inter-GPU comms. Cache hits are checked via a lightweight Bloom filter per remote block to avoid unnecessary requests.
3) Async prefetch + pipelined reduction: When non-local blocks are required, issue asynchronous NCCL point-to-point (cudaMemcpyAsync+cudaIpc for intra-node) pulls for full KV tensors for the block into pinned staging buffers, then overlap decode+kernel execution with remainder I/O. For attention outputs that need reduction across head shards we use NCCL reduce-scatter followed by local attention apply and an all-gather only when downstream pipeline stage requires full hidden states.
4) Degraded mode: if interconnect bandwidth or latency SLOs are violated (configurable thresholds), automatically switch to CPU-hosted shared KV: remote GPUs push compact compressed blocks (FP16+quantized keys) to a pinned CPU cache and rehydrate on demand; this trades latency for predictable memory usage.
5) Eviction and compaction: background compaction tasks run per node, consolidating small blocks and optionally recompressing to lower precision. Eviction policy is LRU at block granularity with heuristics to keep the most recent N token-blocks local to the GPU serving the active stream.

Implementation details and API changes:
- New runtime module: kv_shard_manager (C++/CUDA) that exposes: configure_sharding(topology_hint, token_block_size, head_block_size), query_block_location(block_id), request_block_async(block_id, callback_token), and evict_block(block_id).
- Add Bloom filters and block metadata to the per-model manifest; expose diagnostics via Console (per-route KV hit-rate, bytes pulled, pending requests).
- Scheduler change: continuous-batcher will prefer co-locating requests with similar prefix-blocks onto GPUs that host those blocks; add a route-aware affinity hint to smart routing.
- NCCL group composition: create intra-stage NCCL groups optimized for head reductions and inter-stage groups for token-block transfers; fall back to host staging when cross-node links are oversubscribed.

Benchmarks and acceptance criteria (initial targets):
- 2x reduction in peak KV memory per GPU for 32k-context models on a 4xA100 node with TP=2, PP=2 (measured with streaming 1k token prefixes across 200 concurrent streams).
- P95 token latency increase <= 10% in steady state when using local fast-path; P99 increase <= 20% relative to baseline replication for workloads with >75% local block hit rate.
- Continuous-batcher throughput should not degrade by more than 5% for high-concurrency steady workloads.

Testing plan and rollout:
- Synthetic unit tests for mapping, Bloom false-positive rates, eviction and compaction correctness.
- Integration test harness that runs model generation across TP/PP topologies (TP:1..4, PP:1..4) with deterministic prefixes and measures memory, NCCL traffic, latency.
- Canary rollout in dedicated infra: enable kv_shard_manager with token_block_size=256 for a small set of internal routes and compare metrics in Console.
- Gradual enable via rollout policy: start with read-only (monitor-only) mode -> optimistic prefetch -> active sharding.

Open questions and decisions to be made:
- Optimal default token_block_size across model families (GPT-like vs Dense Transfomer). Plan: run sweep in next perf cycle.
- Bloom filter sizing trade-offs vs false positive overhead. Default currently set to 1% FPR; revisit after benchmarks.
- CPU-hosted degraded mode compression format (INT8 vs product quantization).
